Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Boun had managed the downtown hotel for twenty-two years, a tenure built on his unflappable calm and meticulous attention to detail. Now, at sixty, that foundation had crumbled. The man who sat in the therapy office was a stranger to the one who had once prided himself on handling any crisis. Eight months ago, a new hire in the laundry room had, in a moment of panic over a large stain, mixed two industrial cleaning agents. The resulting chloramine gas filled the enclosed basement space in seconds. Boun had been the first to respond to the frantic call, rushing in to pull the choking young man out. In those few moments, the air was thick with a sharp, metallic tang that burned his throat and sinuses. He remembers the taste more than anything—acrid, chemical, the taste of poison. He got the employee out, but not before inhaling enough to leave him gasping on the concrete floor, his own body feeling alien and overwhelmed.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel like a minefield. The memory of the event was not something he could choose to recall; it would ambush him without warning. Walking past the housekeeping carts in the hallway, the faint scent of bleach was enough to trigger it. Suddenly, he would be back in the basement, the raw, metallic taste flooding his mouth as if he were breathing in the fumes all over again. His heart would hammer against his ribs, his lungs would feel tight, and for a terrifying minute, the polished hotel corridor would dissolve, replaced by the damp, grey walls of the laundry room. He felt he was truly reliving it, a helpless passenger in his own mind. He had come to believe his body was no longer a reliable vessel but a traitor, permanently damaged and poised to fail him at any moment. He found himself constantly taking his own pulse, checking his tongue in the reflection of his phone screen for discoloration, and interpreting every cough or tickle in his throat as a sign that the poison was finally winning.

His work, once a source of pride, became a landscape of perceived threats. Boun’s daily rounds transformed from quality control inspections into painstaking threat assessments. He would scan every corner, every closet, every cart, his body perpetually coiled and tense, ready for a danger he was certain was lurking just out of sight. He insisted on new, complicated protocols for chemical storage that his staff found bewildering and inefficient. When a room service delivery took five minutes longer than scheduled, his mind didn't jump to a slow elevator; it jumped to a collapsed employee, another victim he had failed to protect. He was convinced that he was powerless to stop bad things from happening, that disaster was always imminent. His constant state of alert was exhausting, leaving him with a bone-deep weariness that sleep could not touch. At home, his partner Soriya would watch him with worried eyes, but any attempt she made to talk about the "incident" was met with a curt shutdown. He couldn't bear to hear it mentioned; being reminded by others felt like being pushed back into the gas-filled room.

The space between Boun and the world grew wider. He felt disconnected from his staff, who now treated him with a cautious distance. He felt estranged from Soriya, unable to share the terror that governed his days. This isolation fed a gnawing belief that he no longer belonged anywhere—not in the hotel he had run for decades, not in the home he had shared for years, not even in his own skin. He finally sought help after a particularly frightening episode at work. A guest had broken a bottle of strong, floral perfume in the lobby. The chemical scent, though entirely different, sent Boun into a full-blown panic. He stumbled into his office, gasping for air, the phantom taste of bleach and ammonia filling his mouth, absolutely convinced he was being poisoned all over again. The false alarm was so powerful, so real, that he realized he could no longer distinguish between memory and reality. He was terrified of losing his mind completely, and even more terrified of living the rest of his life as a prisoner to that single moment in the basement.
